deck.title: FreeRTOS on ESP32
deck.subtitle: Concurrency without mystery reboots · T8 teaching deck
deck.purpose: The explanation portion of T8, delivered before the hands-on refactor. Covers tasks, stack sizing, cores, queues, mutexes, event-driven input, stack-overflow forensics and the watchdog. Pairs with introduction_deck.json.
deck.position_in_course: Day 3, Topic 8 — after T7 (RS485), before the T9 mini project

design_direction.tone: Technical and direct. This audience knows what a scheduler is — do not explain preemption from first principles. Spend the time on the ESP32-specific facts they will get wrong.

slides.title: FreeRTOS on ESP32
slides.subtitle: Concurrency without mystery reboots
slides.meta: T8 · Day 3 · ~35 min explanation, then refactor
slides.speaker_notes: This is the deep-dive topic for this cohort. Do not rush it — the room is senior enough to want the details.

slides.statement:
You have been running FreeRTOS
all week.
slides.caption: `loop()` is not the metal. It is a task the Arduino core created for you.
slides.speaker_notes: Open with this. It reframes everything that follows as 'taking control of something already there', not 'adding an RTOS'.

slides.title: What the Arduino core actually does

callout.text: Your whole week of code has been one task, priority 1, pinned to Core 1.

slides.speaker_notes: Ask the room what priority they think loop() runs at. Almost nobody guesses '1, barely above idle'.

slides.title: Why one big loop stops scaling

columns.heading: The T6 device today
columns.body: One `loop()` juggling six responsibilities on `millis()` timers · every new feature adds another timer and another branch · the slowest thing in the loop sets the latency for everything else · nothing is independently testable

columns.heading: What tasks buy you
columns.body: Each responsibility gets its own flow of control, its own rate, its own priority · the alarm can preempt the display · new hardware becomes a new task, not a new branch in a 400-line loop

slides.speaker_notes: Frame the refactor as maintainability and latency, not performance. Nothing gets faster; things get predictable and reviewable.

slides.title: Creating a task — every argument matters
slides.speaker_notes: Walk all seven arguments. Then point out the for(;;) — a task function that returns without vTaskDelete() crashes the system.

slides.title: Argument 3 — the stack size trap
slides.subtitle: This is the single most expensive misunderstanding in the topic.

items.text: **Vanilla FreeRTOS takes stack depth in WORDS.** Most tutorials, most Stack Overflow answers, and most AI output assume this.
**ESP32 takes it in BYTES.** A number that is 'safe' in a generic example is **4× too small** here.
**`1024` is the AI's favourite default.** That is 1 KB. Add a `Serial.printf`, an ArduinoJson document, or any driver call and it overflows.
**The symptom is not a stack error.** It is a boot loop, or resets that look exactly like a bad USB cable or a failing board.

callout.text: Engineers lose afternoons to this, blaming hardware. You will deliberately cause it later in this topic.

slides.speaker_notes: This is the headline trap of T8. Say the word BYTES loudly. Everything in stage 5 pays this off.

slides.title: Priority — and what it actually means
rows: must be allowed to run — the watchdog watches it

callout.text: Higher number = more urgent. A higher-priority task that never yields will starve everything below it — including idle.

slides.speaker_notes: Common AI failure: every task created at the same priority, or the alarm task lowest. Ask the room which task in their device deserves to preempt the others.

slides.title: Task states

diagram.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Ready: xTaskCreate
    Ready --> Running: scheduler picks it
    Running --> Ready: preempted by higher priority
    Running --> Blocked: vTaskDelay / queue wait / mutex wait
    Blocked --> Ready: timeout or event
    Running --> Suspended: vTaskSuspend
    Suspended --> Ready: vTaskResume
    Running --> [*]: vTaskDelete

callout.text: **Blocked is the goal.** A blocked task costs zero CPU. Busy-waiting costs everything.

slides.speaker_notes: The one idea to land: waiting should be Blocked, not spinning. Every queue receive and mutex take in this deck is a way to block productively.

slides.title: Two cores — and who already lives there

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TB subgraph C0["Core 0 — PRO_CPU"] W["WiFi + Bluetooth stack
already busy — do not starve"] end subgraph C1["Core 1 — APP_CPU"] L["loopTask (Arduino)"] T["your tasks"] end style C0 fill:#422006,stroke:#FBBF24,color:#FDE68A style C1 fill:#0C4A6E,stroke:#38BDF8,color:#E0F2FE

bullets: **Core 0** runs the WiFi/BT stack — pin heavy work here and MQTT starts dropping
**Core 1** runs `loop()` by default — your tasks belong here
`tskNO_AFFINITY` lets the scheduler choose
**A 'network problem' is often a scheduling problem**
slides.speaker_notes: This failure is worth demonstrating if time allows: pin a busy task to Core 0 and watch MQTT get flaky. It looks exactly like a broker or AP fault.

slides.title: `delay()` vs `vTaskDelay()` — get this right

columns.heading: The myth
columns.body:
"`delay()` blocks the whole chip and starves other tasks."

The AI will tell you this. On ESP32 Arduino it is **not true** — `delay()` wraps `vTaskDelay()`, so it *does* yield.

columns.heading: What is actually true
columns.body:
`delay()` still stalls **that task's own work** — your no-`delay()` rule was always about your own responsiveness.

`vTaskDelay()` states the intent clearly in task code.

⚠ `delayMicroseconds()` **busy-waits and does not yield.**

callout.text: The real starvation risk is a loop with no delay and no yield at all — that trips the task watchdog.

slides.speaker_notes: Be precise here. Repeating the myth costs credibility with this audience, and the nuance is a genuine catch-the-AI: it will confidently over-claim.

slides.title: Why not just a shared global?

columns.heading: The tempting version
columns.body:
`float g_temp;`

Sensor task writes it, network task reads it. The AI will tell you this is fine.

It is a **race**: a multi-byte write can be preempted halfway. `volatile` prevents the compiler caching it — it does **not** make the access atomic.

columns.heading: The correct version
columns.body:
A **queue**: a thread-safe FIFO that copies your data.

The reader **blocks** until something arrives — no polling, no spinning, no torn reads.

It also decouples rates: the producer and consumer need not agree on timing.

slides.speaker_notes: The volatile misconception is widespread even among experienced engineers. Say plainly: volatile is about the compiler, not about concurrency.

slides.title: Queues in practice

callout.text: Timeout 0 = never block. portMAX_DELAY = block forever. Both are decisions — make them deliberately.

slides.speaker_notes: Push on queue-full policy: drop newest, drop oldest, or block the producer? There is no default right answer, which is exactly why the AI picking one silently is a problem.

slides.title: Mutex — one bus, several tasks
bullets: An I²C transaction is **several bus operations** — preempt it halfway and both callers get garbage
You will create this contention yourself when the gesture task lands
Remove the mutex deliberately and watch reads garble and gestures vanish
**The AI's fix for bus corruption is "add a delay."** That is not a fix
slides.speaker_notes: Emphasise: a delay makes the race less likely, not impossible. That distinction is the whole point of a mutex.

slides.title: Event-driven input — the gesture task
bullets: Not every task is periodic — some should **wait for something to happen**
A gesture task blocks on the sensor, then posts an **event** to a queue
No polling in the main loop, no missed input between timer ticks
Same discipline as an ISR: **detect, post, get out** — do the work elsewhere
This is the task you add *after* the structure exists, to prove how cheap it is

callout.text: Watch how few files change when you add it. That is the return on the refactor.

prio 4 · highest"] G["gesture task

callout.text: Five tasks · two queues · one mutex · an essentially empty `loop()`.

slides.speaker_notes: Put this on the board and leave it up during the build. Participants should draw their own version in Stage 0 before prompting.

slides.title: The instrument: high-water mark
bullets: It is a **low-water mark**: the worst case seen since boot, not the current free space
Run the device through its heaviest path *before* you trust the number
Size from **measurement**, then leave headroom — not from a guessed default
A number close to zero is a crash that has not happened yet

callout.text: Both `xTaskCreate`'s stack argument and this return value are in BYTES on ESP32 — unlike vanilla FreeRTOS docs.

slides.speaker_notes: Have them add this to every task from the start, not at the end. It is the difference between engineering and guessing.

slides.title: Stack overflow — what it looks like from outside

columns.heading: What you observe
columns.body:
Random resets · boot loop · "works until it doesn't" · fails only when the network is busy or a log line is longer than usual

**It looks exactly like a bad USB cable, a flaky board, or a weak supply.**

columns.heading: What it actually is
columns.body:
A task wrote past the end of its stack.

The panic + backtrace names the task. Decode it and the answer is immediate.

**You will cause this deliberately today** — shrink a stack until it panics, and read the output.

callout.text: Have the exception decoder ready. A raw backtrace with no symbols teaches nothing.

slides.speaker_notes: This slide is the reason the topic exists. An engineer who has read one stack-overflow backtrace never loses an afternoon to it again.

slides.title: The task watchdog
bullets: The TWDT watches that the **idle task** on each core still gets to run
A task that loops with **no delay, no yield, no blocking call** starves it
Symptom: `Task watchdog got triggered` naming the offending task
Fix the design — yield, block on a queue, or lower the priority
**Do not** disable the watchdog to make the message go away

callout.text: The AI's suggested fix is often to disable the watchdog. That deletes the warning, not the bug.

slides.title: What to hold on to
bullets: **Stack depth is in BYTES on ESP32** — and `1024` is not a size, it's a guess
**Blocked beats busy** — queues and mutexes let a task wait for free
**`volatile` is about the compiler, not concurrency** — use a queue
**Core 0 belongs to WiFi** — starve it and the network looks broken
**Measure stacks, don't guess** — `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark` on every task
**A mystery reset is a readable backtrace** you haven't decoded yet
slides.closing_statement: Now go and break it on purpose: shrink a stack until it panics, and remove the mutex until the gestures vanish. Both failures are cheap here and expensive in the field.
slides.speaker_notes: Straight into Stage 0 — the paper task map — before anyone opens Devin.

items.text: **Stack too small** — `1024` default, and the words-vs-bytes confusion on top of it.
**Shared globals** declared safe, often without even `volatile`, and never a queue.
**Unguarded I²C from two tasks** — and "add a delay" offered as the fix.
**Gesture I²C address invented** — scan for `0x73`; the datasheet itself says verify.
**Heavy work pinned to Core 0** — MQTT drops and it looks like a network fault.
**Over-claiming about `delay()`** — on ESP32 Arduino it does yield; the real risk is a loop with no yield at all.
**Disabling the watchdog** to silence a symptom instead of fixing the design.
**All tasks at one priority**, or the alarm task lowest.
